analysis.investment_thesis: INOX India is a genuinely high-quality cryogenic equipment business with ROCE of 38%, but the Magic Formula collapses on valuation — Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) of just ~2.1% is roughly six times below the 12% threshold needed for the formula to work. The market has already priced in the quality, leaving no margin of safety.
key_strengths: ROCE of 38% is exceptional — one of the highest-quality businesses in Indian industrials by Greenblatt's return-on-capital metric
Near debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.10), with borrowings declining from INR 145 Cr (2020) to INR 43 Cr net debt currently
Secular tailwinds across LNG, green hydrogen, and aerospace/cryogenic propulsion with consistent 12% revenue CAGR
key_risks: Valuation is the primary killer: EV ≈ INR 13,578 Cr vs EBIT of INR 285 Cr = Earnings Yield of just 2.1%; Magic Formula requires >12%
FCF has collapsed — from INR 225 Cr (2021) to -INR 3 Cr (2025) as capex surged to INR 125 Cr; the business is in heavy investment mode with uncertain return timeline
6-year Net Profit CAGR of only 2.7% (INR 193 Cr in 2019 → INR 226 Cr in 2025) exposes that reported earnings are supported by lumpy 'other income' rather than pure operating leverage
red_flags: Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) of ~2.1% — roughly 1/6th of Greenblatt's 12% minimum threshold; EV/EBITDA of 41x confirms extreme overvaluation on Magic Formula basis
FCF turned negative in FY2025 (-INR 3 Cr) despite INR 285 Cr EBIT; capex tripled in two years (INR 44 Cr → INR 125 Cr), raising capital efficiency questions
Net Profit CAGR of 2.7% over six years signals significant one-time/other income dependency in early years (FY2019 NP of INR 193 Cr was artificially high)
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on INOX India yields a stark split: the business is excellent, the price is punishing. EBIT of INR 285 Cr against an Enterprise Value of ~INR 13,578 Cr (Market Cap INR 13,539 Cr + Net Debt ~INR 39 Cr) produces an Earnings Yield of just 2.1% — well below the 6% floor I consider minimally acceptable and far from the 12%+ that makes the formula fire. On the other side, ROCE of 38% is genuinely top-decile; the business earns extraordinary returns on the capital it deploys, sustaining 19.6% operating margins on specialty cryogenic equipment that serves LNG, hydrogen, and aerospace clients. The formula requires BOTH legs. With only one, I pass.

The FCF deterioration is a secondary but real concern. Free cash flow has eroded from INR 225 Cr (FY2021) to negative INR 3 Cr (FY2025) as annual capex tripled to INR 125 Cr. This may well be value-creating investment — the addressable market in LNG infrastructure and cryogenic propulsion is expanding — but at 41x EV/EBITDA, the market is already pricing in a flawless execution of that expansion. Greenblatt's edge comes from buying cheap and good simultaneously; at 53x P/E, there is no cheapness buffer. If capex returns normalize and ROIC holds, this stock could re-rate lower even if the business performs fine. I would revisit at Earnings Yield >8% (roughly INR 600–700 price range at current EBIT), where the formula begins to make sense.
